title: Endless Worlds is live: an isometric pixel art MMO I built from scratch with Claude
author: Trexaty92
selftext:
I have been working on this one for a couple of months now, and refining the asset pipeline has been a mission. But I have finally got to a point where I can generate some pretty nifty pixel art and animations with an engine I built from the ground up with Claude's assistance. The map builder was built AI first and has taken more hours than i would like to admit to refine to the point of getting a solid map out of a prompt.

  
[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xrXSZCmLEdQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xrXSZCmLEdQ)

Endless Worlds is a small online RPG inspired by Endless Online. Every map, character and monster in it was made for this game. It's free and runs in the browser, on desktop, or on a phone: [https://www.endless-worlds.com/play](https://www.endless-worlds.com/play)

Right now there are 37 maps, six classes (your weapon decides your class, so pick up a bow and you're a Ranger), gathering trades like mining, woodcutting and fishing.

  
Player characters aren't drawn frame by frame. A body, a garment, a weapon and a head of hair are each modelled once on a 3D rig and then photographed in every pose and facing, so a new coat fits every animation the day it's made. Monsters and NPCs work the same way, posed on a rig and photographed into their sixteen frames, and mounts are proper solid models refined a part at a time. The whole pipeline is plain Python, standard library only ( no blender ).

Maps work on heights. A map says how tall each cell stands, and the wall faces, copings, corners and shadows are all derived from that. Shadows fall on the height field, which is why the same lighting works for a lamp at night and the sun at noon.

  
This is the part I'd point other AI devs at. The builder publishes a probe on the page with the map document, the view and the camera, so Claude can check where something was actually drawn instead of doing the isometric maths in its head and getting it slightly wrong. Its checks count the pixels an overlay puts on screen and confirm they go back to zero. I still build the main town by hand in it, which is the best test it gets.

  
What I'd tell anyone doing this with an AI, with a standard library.

Don't let it reason about visuals from code. It will tell you a sprite faces the right way with total confidence. My rule became that anything that has to look right gets screenshotted off the running game and read back, and that one change fixed more bugs than anything else.. it is a long process but after months of refinement its a wonderful feeling being able to prompt a beautiful map with beautiful npcs into existence reliably.

Watch your CLAUDE.md. Mine got to 124,000 characters before I noticed every session was paying for all of it. It's now under 30k with a hook that warns when it grows past budget, and the detail lives in docs that get loaded when they're needed.

The stack, for the curious: TypeScript everywhere, Node with `ws` and PostgreSQL on the server, PixiJS 8 for the renderer, Electron for desktop, Capacitor for Android, and Nuxt for the map builder, the admin console and the site.

Happy to answer questions about the pipeline or the workflow. Feedback on the game is very welcome too, it's early days.
